headline: Engineer turned conservationist reshaped how India protects its elephants
meta_description: Vinod Rishi, first director of Project Elephant, shifted wildlife management from individual parks to whole landscapes, ensuring elephants could migrate safely…
summary_short: An engineer-turned-forest officer changed how India protects elephants by managing entire migration corridors instead of isolated reserves.
body:
Vinod Rishi spent 38 years in India's forest service fundamentally reshaping how the nation manages its elephants. As the first director of Project Elephant—launched in 1992—he recognized that these animals cannot survive within park boundaries alone. They travel across state lines, through farmland, past irrigation projects, and along ancient routes that now intersect with human development. His insight was practical: wildlife conservation had to address entire landscapes, not isolated reserves. When changes were needed to the Teesta Barrage Project in North Bengal to preserve an elephant corridor, Rishi worked to bring development planning and wildlife conservation together, allowing elephants to continue their passages through the region. This became his signature approach during a career that took him from field postings in West Bengal to India's highest wildlife administration positions.

Rishi's background as an engineer trained at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi shaped his method. He tested official claims and scientific findings against what actually happened on the ground. When newspapers reported a leopard causing panic in a village, he traveled there himself and discovered residents were largely untroubled—the real threats were fires, habitat loss, and encroachment. He brought the same scrutiny to tiger censuses and poaching investigations, willing to listen to evidence gathered by outside conservationists and help them navigate government systems.

After retiring in 2006, Rishi continued advising conservation organizations and mentoring younger forest officers. His later writings revealed an intimate attention to individual animals and the places they inhabited. One story returned repeatedly to the Teesta corridor, explaining not the bureaucratic approvals but the reason those changes mattered: elephants had long passed that way, and because the plans were altered, they still could. Colleagues remembered him as humble and determined—qualities evident in a career devoted not to individual recognition, but to keeping corridors open for creatures that needed room to roam.
quick_facts: First director of Project Elephant, India's national conservation program launched in 1992
Engineer from IIT Delhi who brought evidence-based methods to wildlife management
Worked 38 years in Indian Forest Service across Bengal tiger reserves and national parks
Helped preserve Teesta elephant corridor in North Bengal despite major development project
Wrote Whispers From the Wild, collecting 17 stories from his conservation career
